english: What do you eat at dawn? At dawn I eat meat with butter; my lady (wife) cooks it. What do you eat? I eat honey and I drink water. It is sweet at dawn.
uncertain: last sentence: what h₁íd refers to (honey?)

english: Who are you? I am Good-Fame (h₁suḱléwēs). And who are you? I am Manly-Minded (h₂nr̥ménēs), a guest. Welcome, guest! Sit by my father and drink. May the gods give you good things.
uncertain: names read as compounds 'having good fame', 'having a man's mind'

english: Will you sell me wool? I sell it to you. What do you give me (in payment)? I give you cattle. Cattle? We do not know (want?) cattle. Give me silver, or bring a dog. Now I bring it to you.
uncertain: h₁opéye- read as 'pay, give in exchange'; root not recognised blind
péḱu ne widmé: 'we do not know' (perfect) vs 'we did not see'
h₁íd in last sentence refers to silver or dog

english: Now, friend, I am going home. Don't go! It is getting dark. Lie down here. What do you (pl.) eat? We eat meat with butter. Now I sit (down).
uncertain: h₁édte read as 2PL, though the addressee is a single friend

english: What gifts do you give to guests? He who took a gift gives a gift. My father gave many gifts, and he has many friends. Now I give you a gift. Guest, your word is sweet to me.
uncertain: h₁áyto / h₁áyt as middle 'took' vs active 'gave' (h₁ay- 'give/take')
déh₃ōr vs dóh₃r̥: two different forms for 'gift' in one text

english: My sons have not eaten today. Lead them inside. The women are cooking for me. You are kind to us. Father Sky protects guests. May he protect you.
uncertain: pótn̥yeh₂su LOC.PL 'among the ladies' — sense of the sentence unclear
ḱósmi dinóy read as 'on this day'
